title: Yud
hookLine: the smallest letter, which begins God's name

lines: A DROP HANGING FROM THE LINE.
cards: On a page of Hebrew, the letters sit on the line and fill the space between top and bottom. One doesn't.
It hangs from the top line like a drop of water that hasn't fallen yet: a short stroke, a little hook, hardly more than a comma. You could miss it. A scribe writing a Torah scroll can't.
And this tiny mark has a double life. It begins a word scribes treat with special care, the name of God.
And it's the hero of a tender story the rabbis tell, about a letter that went missing and wouldn't stop asking to be used.

teach.b: First, the name. The holy name of God in the Torah, which the King James renders LORD in capital letters, begins with a yud. Jewish tradition treats that name with such care that it isn't spoken aloud as written.

In prayer and Torah reading, Jews traditionally say Adonai, my Lord, in its place, and in ordinary talk some say Hashem, the Name. So the smallest letter stands at the front of the word held with such care.
Second, a story. Remember Sarai becoming Sarah? The yud at the end of her name came off to make room.
The rabbis, in the Jerusalem Talmud, imagine what happened to it. The little yud came before God and complained: I was in the name of a righteous woman, and now I've been taken out.

It kept asking, for a long time, until God placed it at the front of another name. In Numbers, Moses sends scouts into the land and renames one of them. In the King James: "And Moses called Oshea the son of Nun Jehoshua."
Hoshea becomes Yehoshua, Joshua. A yud added to the front. The lost letter found its place.
Third, why tell it. It's a story about something small refusing to be wasted; the rabbis wouldn't let even one letter fall off the page and be forgotten.
A lot of any day is yud-sized: a text answered, a dish washed, a name remembered.
Small isn't the same as unimportant.

how: Jews traditionally do not pronounce God's holy name as written: in prayer and Torah reading it is read as Adonai, and in everyday speech some say Hashem, 'the Name'. Scribes writing a Torah scroll must form every letter, even the tiny yud, correctly.

games.q: you're the yud taken off the end of Sarai's name when she became Sarah. what do you do, in the rabbis' story?
o: keep asking God until you're placed in another name.
go back and push out the heh.
games.why: the yud complains before God until it's placed at the front of Hoshea's name, making Yehoshua, Joshua (Numbers 13:16).

practice: Pick something tiny you'll do today anyway: making the bed, pouring a glass of water, folding one shirt.

In your mind, do it slowly and completely, the way a scribe forms a yud, the whole of your attention on something nobody else may ever notice; if you pray, offer that small act as part of your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Yud. The smallest letter, which begins God's holy name, and in the rabbis' story moved from Sarai's name to Joshua's. Today's word.
